title: KV paging and memory-bandwidth profiling notes
content:
Summary:

This working doc captures profiling runs and hypotheses about KV cache paging/eviction causing runtime slowdowns under certain workloads. Focus is on reuse rates, eviction spikes, and observed host<->GPU traffic that looks like paging (PCIe/CPU mem copies) and possible memory-bandwidth saturation on GPUs.

Context / why we care:
- Some customers see latency regressions on long-context LLM workloads (seq_len > 1024) on Dedicated nodes.
- We suspect the KV cache pressure is triggering frequent evictions and host-side paging that increases per-token latency and jitter.
- Goal: determine whether (and when) eviction/paging is the dominant contributor to latency; quantify how much bandwidth is consumed and whether GPU memory bandwidth or PCIe is the limiting factor.

Quick findings (TL;DR):
- Reuse rates drop from ~84% to ~37% when sequence length increases from 512->2048 in our synthetic chat replay workload.
- Eviction events correlate with increased PCIe traffic measured by nvlink/nvml tools: observed ~8-12 GB/s sustained PCIe transfer during high-eviction periods (on our 1xA100 host), and GPU DRAM bandwidth utilization rises by ~10-18% compared to baseline.
- End-to-end per-token latency increases by ~18–32% when eviction/paging is happening vs. steady-state cache hits.
- CPU-side page-faults are not dominant, but memcpy kernel time and GPU memcpy stalls increase significantly (flame graphs show memcopy hotspots).

Repro recipe (toy workload):
1) Start dedicated serving process with model variant quantized-8-bit, single worker, config: batch_size=1, max_seq=2048, kv_cache_enabled=true, cache_capacity=12GB (on 40GB GPU).
2) Run synthetic client that replays a mix of conversations: 80% short contexts (<=256), 20% long context prepends (>=1536). Profile for 30 minutes.
3) Tools to run (on same node):
   - nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o T -d 1 > /tmp/gpu_dmon.log
   - NVTX regions enabled in runtime for "KV_EVICT" and "KV_LOAD"
   - sudo perf record -g -p <serving_pid> -o /tmp/perf.data -- sleep 120
   - python -m pyinstrument --include-serving --outfile /tmp/pyinstr.html --pid <serving_pid> (if Python runtime)
   - collect /proc/vmstat, /proc/meminfo, and `cat /proc/<pid>/status` snapshots before/during/after
   - capture NIC and PCIe counters via NVML or nvidia-smi pmon

Commands we used: (examples from runs)
- nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1 > run1_gpu_dmon.tsv &
- sudo perf record -e cycles:u -g -p 2345 -o /tmp/perf_evict.data -- sleep 180
- python tools/kv_profiler.py --sample-interval 0.5 --pid 2345 --out /tmp/kv_sample.csv

Observations from single-run (2025-01-20 run):
- At t=00:05 into the workload we see eviction burst markers from runtime NVTX: KV_EVICT start/end pairs every ~120ms for ~3s window. During that window:
  - nvidia-smi dmon shows GPU memory utilization unchanged but PCIe RX increases to ~10.2 GB/s sustained.
  - perf flamegraph (collapsed) shows memcpy_avx512 and gpu_memcpy_host_to_device as top stacks during those epochs.
  - p99 latency spikes from 78ms -> 104ms.
- Reuse rate metric (reported by instrumentation): cache_lookups=1.2M, cache_hits=444k => reuse_rate ~37% (compared to steady-state ~84% during earlier epoch).
- Host CPU usage increases ~12% in memcpy-heavy threads; GPU SM utilization drops slightly (~5%) indicating stalls waiting on data movement.

Microbenchmarks (isolated):
- Local memcopy test (host->gpu) measured with cudaMemcpyAsync shows ~11.4 GB/s over PCIe for 16MB chunks, consistent with observed runtime transfers. This suggests that the runtime is not saturating raw PCIe ceiling but is doing repeated medium-sized transfers that add latency.
- GPU DRAM bandwidth (measured with microbench) shows headroom; peaks during eviction windows increase but do not hit theoretical max. Suggests PCIe/PCIe transactions + memcpy overhead and kernel scheduling are the larger factor.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Eviction churn due to insufficient per-model cache partitioning: different conversations thrash a shared cache leading to many small host<->device transfers.
2) Runtime is using suboptimal transfer sizes (many small memcpy calls) instead of coalescing eviction pages leading to inefficient PCIe utilization and higher latency.
3) Frequent cache warming loads (loading KV fragments back to GPU on short tails) cause memcpy stalls and displace working set, reducing reuse rate.
4) NUMA/CPU placement: memcpy threads pinned to cpu sockets not local to the NIC/NVLink create higher latency for transfers for nodes with host memory involvement.

Evidence for hypothesis 1 & 2:
- Stack traces show many repeated memcpy calls from eviction logic rather than one aggregated transfer.
- When we artificially increase the eviction batch threshold (in runtime config) to coalesce 8 pages before issuing transfer, PCIe transfer rate jumps to ~20 GB/s bursts but overall p99 latency drops ~7% because amortized overhead reduces. Reuse rate increases slightly (cache hammering reduced).

Counter-evidence / things that don't match:
- We did not see increased major page faults or OOM killer activity; host page faults stable.
- GPU DRAM bandwidth not fully saturated, so pure DRAM bandwidth cap is unlikely the limiting factor.

Detailed timelines (extract from run):
- 00:00-02:00 baseline warmup: reuse_rate ~82-86%, p50 ~21ms, p99 ~79ms
- 02:00-02:03 eviction burst window: reuse_rate falls to 38%, p99 -> 102ms
- 02:03-05:00 recovery: reuse climbs back to ~70% after active cache warming; p99 declines back to ~84ms

What to measure next (concrete experiments):
- A: Vary eviction coalescing threshold (1,2,4,8 pages aggregated). Measure per-token latency, PCIe bandwidth patterns, and reuse_rate.
- B: Pin memcpy/eviction threads to different NUMA nodes and compare latencies. Use numactl and hwloc mapping.
- C: Introduce a simulated background bandwidth consumer (iperf/cpu memcpy) to see if competing host memory bandwidth materially degrades eviction time.
- D: Trace-level: add unique eviction IDs in NVTX and correlate client request IDs -> eviction transfers to see which requests cause the most pressure.

Potential mitigations (prototype ideas):
- Aggressive coalescing of KV eviction/loads into fewer larger DMA ops. Tradeoff: bursts that may raise instantaneous PCIe bandwidth but reduce per-op overhead.
- Per-conversation shard/partitioning for KV to reduce cross-conversation eviction churn. Might increase memory footprint but improve reuse.
- Adaptive eviction thresholds driven by reuse-rate heuristics: when reuse drops, increase patience/coalescing.
- Pre-fetching for long-tail replays: detect repeated access patterns and keep a small pinned working set on GPU.

Open questions and unknowns:
- Is NVLink vs PCIe behavior different on multi-GPU nodes with NVLink present? Our current runs are single-GPU. Need to repeat on 8xA100 DGX-style node.
- How much does model quantization / KV compression affect transfer size and frequency? Does 4-bit quant lead to smaller transfers but more CPU decompression overhead?
- Are there edge cases where coalescing hurts latency for very low-latency workloads (batch_size=1, p50 sensitive)? We need micro-SLO tests.

Next action items (owners):
- Daniel: run experiment A (eviction coalescing 1/2/4/8) across three models (m1-small, m2-base, m3-large) and collect metrics. Due 2025-02-07.
- Marta: NUMA pinning runs on Dedicated node type D2 and document differences. Due 2025-02-06.
- Owen: Instrumentation: add per-eviction NVTX ids and extend kv_profiler to emit pairing (evict_id -> request_ids). Due 2025-02-04.
- Aisha: Pull together result dashboard and prepare short write-up for eng retro. Due 2025-02-10.

Notes / random troubleshooting observations:
- Flaky observation: sometimes evictions show up as GPU->host transfers instead of host->GPU. Hypothesis: runtime resizes cache and writes cold shards to host for persistence. Need to confirm code path.
- Increasing CUDA stream priority for memcpy stream reduced some p99 spikes; suggests scheduling contention between compute and DMA streams. Might be a knob: prioritize compute stream or use dedicated copy engine.

Raw metric excerpts (from run):
- cache_lookups: 1203456
- cache_hits: 444012
- reuse_rate: 0.369
- eviction_ops_total: 3124
- avg_evict_pages_per_op: 2.1
- pci_rx_gb_s_peak: 11.2
- gpu_dram_bandwidth_used_pct_peak: 37.4
- p50_latency_ms_baseline: 21.3
- p99_latency_ms_during_eviction: 103.7

Appendix: useful links and notes
- NVML counters: https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/nvml-api/
- perf flamegraph workflow: https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph
- Relevant code area: serving/runtime/kv_cache/{evictor.cpp, transfer_manager.cpp}
- Related Jira: RINF-1423 (investigate eviction-induced latency)

If you run the repro and get different results, paste the kv_profiler CSV here and I will re-run the analysis script.

-- Aisha
